A2.text:
Samir is nine. He only likes fast 3D computer games. Last rainy Sunday in Baku, his uncle Rauf visited and brought an old box of films. “Look at this,” Rauf said. “It is an animated film from my childhood — ‘Jirtdan’.”

Samir was not excited. “Old cartoons are slow,” he said. “The storyline is always for babies.”

Rauf smiled and started the film. For Rauf, it was full of nostalgia. “Good art can take someone back thirty years in one second,” he said. On the screen, a clever little boy and a giant appeared, drawn frame by frame by hand.

Then a red fox walked onto the screen and spoke. The villain had a funny, musical voice. Suddenly, Samir looked at his uncle. “Wait! That voiceover sounds like you!”

Rauf laughed. “In 1995, I was a young actor. When they dubbed the new version, I gave my voice to the fox. Every actor wanted the character to come to life and feel larger than life.”

Rauf stood up and did the fox's voice in the living room. Samir could not stop laughing. That afternoon, they drew twenty pictures on a small notebook and flipped the pages fast to make their own fox run.

questions.q: What is the story mainly about?
options: A boy who discovers that his uncle voiced a cartoon fox and falls in love with hand-drawn animation
How to make a 3D computer game in Baku
A boy who loses his uncle's old box of films
Why children should not watch television on Sundays
questions.why: Samir thinks old cartoons are boring until he hears his uncle's voice as the fox and draws a flipbook with him.

questions.q: Why did Samir not want to watch the old cartoon at first?
options: He thought old cartoons were slow and for babies
He had already seen it ten times
He wanted to play football outside
questions.why: “Old cartoons are slow,” he said. “The storyline is always for babies.”

questions.q: What did Samir and Rauf make at the end of the afternoon?
options: A twenty-page notebook drawing where the fox ran when they flipped the pages
questions.why: “They drew twenty pictures on a small notebook and flipped the pages fast to make their own fox run.”

questions.q: Uncle Rauf drew the pictures for the 1995 film himself.
questions.why: Rauf was a voice actor who gave his voice to the fox, not the artist who drew it.

questions.q: Every actor wanted the fox to “come to life”. What does “come to life” mean?
options: Seem real and full of energy
questions.why: By using a funny, musical voice, Rauf made a drawing on paper feel like a real living character.

questions.q: How did Samir's opinion of hand-drawn cartoons change by the end?
options: He became curious and excited enough to try drawing animation himself
He was scared of the fox
He wanted to watch it without sound
questions.why: Instead of going back to his games, he spent the afternoon drawing twenty frames of a running fox.

B1.text:
Nine-year-old Samir was convinced that anything made before 2020 was prehistoric. So when a rainy Sunday kept him indoors in Baku and his uncle Rauf put an old Azerbaijani animated film on the television, Samir sighed loudly. “There are no explosions,” he complained. “And the storyline is probably for five-year-olds.”

Rauf only smiled. For him, the opening flute music was pure nostalgia. “Careful,” he said. “One minute of this can take someone back thirty years.” On the screen, painted backgrounds of forests and mountains appeared, every movement drawn by hand, frame by frame.

Five minutes in, the story's villain — a sly red fox in a waistcoat — trotted out from behind a rock and began to speak. Samir froze with a biscuit halfway to his mouth. “Uncle Rauf... why does that fox sound like you when you're pretending to be angry?”

Rauf burst out laughing. “Because it is me. Back in the nineties, I worked in a small recording studio. We dubbed foreign cartoons in the morning, and in the afternoon we recorded voices for local ones. When you do a voiceover, you have to make a flat drawing come to life — every gesture has to sound larger than life.”

To prove it, Rauf stood in front of the television and performed the fox's entire speech from memory, complete with the laugh at the end. Samir was delighted.

When the film finished, the console stayed off. Instead, uncle and nephew sat at the kitchen table with a thick pad of sticky notes, drawing twenty tiny foxes — each paw a millimetre higher on the next page — and flipping the corner until the paper fox ran across the table.

questions.q: What brings Samir and his uncle closer together on the rainy Sunday?
options: Discovering that Uncle Rauf voiced the cartoon villain and making a flipbook animation together
Going to a cinema in the centre of Baku
questions.why: Samir recognises Rauf's voice in the old film, and they spend the rest of the day drawing a running fox on sticky notes.

questions.q: What were the two parts of Rauf's studio job in the nineties?
options: Dubbing foreign cartoons in the morning and recording local voices in the afternoon
Teaching children and playing the flute
questions.why: “We dubbed foreign cartoons in the morning, and in the afternoon we recorded voices for local ones.”

questions.q: How did they make the paper fox move at the kitchen table?
options: They scanned it into a computer
They drew each paw a millimetre higher on each sticky note and flipped the corner
They cut it out with scissors
They used a torch on the wall
questions.why: “Drawing twenty tiny foxes — each paw a millimetre higher on the next page — and flipping the corner.”

questions.q: Rauf needed to read the script from a book to remember the fox's speech.
questions.why: He “performed the fox's entire speech from memory”.

questions.q: Rauf says that one minute of the music can “take someone back thirty years”. What does this mean?
options: Make someone vividly remember the past
Delay the film by half an hour
questions.why: It is linked to nostalgia: the flute music immediately reminds Rauf of his youth.

questions.q: Why does the author mention that “the console stayed off” at the end?
options: The electricity had gone out in the rain
Rauf forbade Samir from playing games
Samir found making his own hand-drawn animation more exciting than his 3D games
questions.why: At the start Samir thought anything before 2020 was prehistoric; by the end he chooses paper and pencil over his console.

B2.text:
To nine-year-old Samir, anything rendered in fewer than sixty frames a second belonged in a museum. So when an October downpour trapped him indoors in Baku and his uncle Rauf queued up a restored Azerbaijani animated short from the nineties, Samir slumped into the corner of the sofa with theatrical martyrdom. The painted colours looked soft, the music came from an actual wooden flute, and he strongly doubted the storyline would contain a single laser.

For Rauf, of course, those opening notes were pure nostalgia; a familiar melody has a way of being able to take someone back three decades before the title card has even faded. On screen, a small mountain village unfolded in watercolour, every shadow and blinking eye drawn by hand, frame by painstaking frame.

Three minutes in, the story's minor villain — a theatrical red fox in a patched waistcoat — stepped out from behind a mulberry tree, dusted his paws and cleared his throat. Samir sat bolt upright. “Wait a second. Why does that fox sound exactly like you when you lose at backgammon?”

Rauf grinned. “Because in 1996 they paid me forty manats and two plates of hot qutab to do the voiceover. We worked in a tiny basement studio near Nizami Cinema — in the mornings we dubbed Brazilian television series into Azerbaijani, and in the afternoons we recorded cartoons. With a drawn character, your voice has to do half the drawing; unless you make him larger than life in front of the microphone, the ink on the paper never really manages to come to life on the screen.”

At Samir's insistence, Rauf stood by the bookcase and delivered the fox's entire monologue word for word, right down to the wheezing laugh at the end.

The game console was not switched on once that afternoon. Instead, they cleared the tea glasses from the table, split a yellow pad of sticky notes in two and spent two quiet hours drawing twenty-four slightly different foxes — discovering that magic, when you flip the corner fast enough with your thumb, still requires nothing more than paper and patience.

words.phrase: before the title card has even faded

questions.q: What is the main point of the story?
options: Old Azerbaijani studios paid voice actors very poorly
A personal human connection reveals the craft and magic behind traditional hand-drawn animation to a sceptical child
Modern video games are harmful to children's imagination
Dubbing foreign series is harder than recording cartoons
questions.why: Hearing his uncle's voice inside a hand-drawn fox transforms Samir's boredom into wonder and hands-on creation.

questions.q: What was Rauf paid for recording the fox's voice in 1996?
options: Forty manats and two plates of qutab
questions.why: “In 1996 they paid me forty manats and two plates of qutab to do the voiceover.”

questions.q: According to Rauf, why does a voice actor have to perform so expressively for animation?
options: Because studio microphones in the nineties were weak
Because the voice has to do half the drawing so the ink can come to life on screen
Because children do not read subtitles
Because the director cannot see the actor
questions.why: “Your voice has to do half the drawing; unless you make him larger than life... the ink never really manages to come to life.”

questions.q: The basement studio near Nizami Cinema is still open today.
questions.why: Rauf describes working there in 1996, but the text never says whether the studio still exists.

questions.q: Unless you make the character “larger than life”, the ink never comes to life. What does “larger than life” mean?
options: More vivid, expressive and dramatic than an ordinary person
questions.why: Rauf contrasts a flat ink drawing with a bold, theatrical vocal performance that gives it personality.

questions.q: Why does the author compare “sixty frames a second” at the beginning with “twenty-four slightly different foxes” at the end?
options: To show that Samir has discovered the same illusion of movement in his own hands that powers his modern games
To prove that twenty-four frames is faster than sixty
To explain how television screens are repaired
To show that Samir is bad at mathematics
questions.why: Samir begins by dismissing anything under 60 fps, then delights in creating movement himself with 24 paper frames.

podcast.title: I always loved the villain

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: What was your favourite cartoon as a child? Guess: who in this episode always liked the bad character — Leyla or Sam?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is cartoons and animation. And yesterday I watched a cartoon with my niece.
Which one?
An old one — the one I loved when I was eight. And I was much more excited than she was!
[laugh] That's nostalgia. One song from a cartoon can take someone back thirty years.
Exactly. In the first minute I remembered every character and almost every line.
When I was a child, our cartoons were always dubbed. The characters spoke Russian or Turkish, never English.
So the famous mouse spoke Turkish?
[chuckle] Yes, with a very deep voice. Years later I heard the English voiceover and I was shocked.
My favourite character was never the hero. I always loved the villain.
Why the villain?
Villains are larger than life. Big voice, big plans, big eyebrows. The hero is often a bit boring.
True. But the storyline needs a good hero too, or there's no story.
Fair. And did you know that a long animated film has more than a hundred thousand frames?
A hundred thousand? Someone draws all of them?
In the old days, yes — by hand. Twenty-four drawings for every second.
That's amazing. And when the pictures move, they really come to life.
Now computers do a lot of the work, but artists still plan every frame.
I think cartoons aren't only for children. The best ones make adults cry.
[sigh] Don't remind me. I cried at the cinema last year. Next to my niece. She wasn't crying.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what cartoon did you love as a child — and who was your favourite character?
Mine was the villain, of course. See you next time!
Bye for now!

questions.q: What is the episode mainly about?
options: Childhood cartoons, characters and how animation is made
questions.why: Nostalgia, dubbed cartoons, villains and frames.

questions.q: What language did the cartoons speak when Leyla was a child?
questions.why: "The characters spoke Russian or Turkish, never English."

questions.q: How many drawings are there for every second of an old animated film?
questions.why: "Twenty-four drawings for every second."

questions.q: Sam's niece cried at the cinema.
questions.why: "She wasn't crying." Sam was.

questions.q: If something is "larger than life", it is…
options: Bigger, louder and more exciting than normal
questions.why: Big voice, big plans, big eyebrows.

questions.q: Why was Sam more excited than his niece?
options: The cartoon was new to him
It reminded him of his childhood
questions.why: It was the cartoon he loved when he was eight — nostalgia.

talk: What cartoon did you love as a child — and who was your favourite character?
Do you prefer the hero or the villain in a story? Why?
